question: Which layer of the pleura hugs the outer surface of the lungs tightly?
explanation: You've got this! Think of the visceral pleura as the inner skin that sticks right onto the lung tissue. Great job keeping up with your anatomy! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h1)

question: What happens in the chest when your diaphragm contracts during a breath in?

options.A: The pleural space fills entirely with air
options.B: Positive pressure forces air out of the lungs
options.C: Negative pressure is created to pull air in
options.D: Pressure inside the chest equals atmospheric pressure

explanation: When the diaphragm moves down, it opens up space and lowers the pressure inside, drawing air naturally into your lungs. Beautiful concept to master! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h1)

question: In a condition called hemothorax, what main substance builds up in the pleural space?
explanation: The name gives it a great clue—'hemo' always points to blood! You are doing fantastic learning these clinical terms. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h2)

question: If a patient has a large left-sided tension pneumothorax, which way is the trachea likely to shift?

options.A: Tracheal deviation toward the left side
options.C: Tracheal deviation toward the right side
options.D: No movement of the mediastinal structures

explanation: Think of it like a crowded room: pressure builds up on the left and pushes everything over toward the healthy right side. You're building solid emergency nursing instincts! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h2)

question: What kind of sound do you usually hear when tapping (percussing) over an area filled with fluid like a pleural effusion?
explanation: Fluid dampens the vibration, giving a flat, dull sound instead of a hollow ring. Keep practicing your physical assessment skills—they get easier every day! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h3)

question: Why might a patient with a collapsed lung (pneumothorax) have absent breath sounds on that side?

options.A: Heart sounds are louder than normal lung sounds
options.B: Air in the pleural space separates the lung from the chest wall, muffling sounds
options.C: Inflammation of the trachea prevents air movement
options.D: Bronchial secretions completely block the mainstem bronchi

explanation: Because air is trapped outside the lung, it acts like a thick cushion blocking the sound from reaching your stethoscope. Makes complete sense when you picture it! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h3)

question: What is the main reason a nurse or doctor performs a thoracentesis for a pleural effusion?

options.A: To deliver continuous oxygen directly into the lung tissue
options.B: To permanently seal the pleural space against future leaks
options.C: To measure direct arterial blood pressure inside the thorax
options.D: To remove fluid for diagnostic analysis and relieve pressure

explanation: It's a win-win procedure: we take out some fluid so the lab can test it, and the patient instantly finds it easier to breathe. You're thinking like a real clinician! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h4)

question: Which quick test is most commonly used at the bedside to check for a collapsed lung?
explanation: A quick chest X-ray gives us an immediate picture of what's going on inside the chest cavity. Keep up the great diagnostic thinking! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h4)

question: What is the main job of the water-seal chamber in a chest drainage setup?

options.A: To deliver humidified oxygen directly into the pleural space
options.B: To allow air to escape from the chest while preventing outside air from entering
options.C: To apply high-pressure suction to reinflate collapsed tissue
options.D: To measure the total volume of blood lost over twenty-four hours

explanation: It acts like a smart one-way valve—letting trapped air bubble out, but never letting room air sneak back in. Brilliant piece of bedside engineering! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h5)

question: You notice continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber of a chest tube system. What does this usually mean?

options.A: An expected amount of residual blood loss
options.B: An air leak somewhere in the tubing or insertion site
options.C: Blockage of the chest tube drainage lumen

explanation: While tiny occasional bubbles can be normal, continuous bubbling is like a leaky bicycle tire telling us air is getting in where it shouldn't. Excellent clinical observation! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h5)

question: A patient's chest tube accidentally slips out of the drainage machine. What is your very first nursing move?

options.A: Call the physician immediately before taking action
options.B: Immerse the end of the chest tube in sterile water
options.C: Remove the dressing and inspect the insertion site
options.D: Clamp the chest tube securely with metal hemostats

explanation: Plunging the tube into sterile water instantly recreates a water seal and stops room air from rushing into the chest. Quick thinking saves lives here! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why must a chest drainage system always stay lower than the patient's chest level?

options.A: To ensure the suction motor runs quietly without disturbing the patient
options.B: To use gravity effectively and prevent fluid from flowing backward into the pleural space
options.C: To make it easier for the patient to ambulate around the room
options.D: To prevent the water-seal chamber from evaporating too quickly

explanation: Gravity is our best friend here; keeping the collection box down ensures fluid drains away from the patient, not back into them. You've got a bright future in ward nursing! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T7#GNS213_U2_T7_h6)
